newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia hopes to defeat major cocoa pest.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia hopes to defeat major cocoa pest.

text.p: A simple two-step technique may hold the key to defeating a moth that threatens Indonesia's efforts to boost its cocoa output, a British expert said on Wednesday.
The pod borer moth lays its eggs on the cocoa pod and the larva penetrates the hard shell to feed on the kernel within the bean, which supplies the world with its chocolate.

Entomologist John Mumford of London University's Imperial College said proper harvesting and pruning of cocoa trees had cut yield loss to a mere five percent per hectare in five one-hectare experimental plots on Sulwesi Island.
This compared with 30 to 35 percent in other areas infested with the pod borer, prevalent in some 40,000 hectares (100,000 acres) throughout the country.
The industry sees the pest as a major threat to boosting output in Indonesia, the world's third largest cocoa producer after the Ivory Coast and Ghana.
The chairman of the Indonesia Cocoa Association (Askindo) said on January 14 that Indonesia's cocoa production was expected to rise 10 percent to around 319,000 to 330,000 tonnes in 1997.
The experiment in Sulawesi, which accounts for some 280,000 of the 400,000 hectares under cocoa cultivation in Indonesia, is being carried out by Askindo and the American Cocoa Research Institute.
Project manager Halim Razak said it was the first time the two groups had linked up to tackle the problem of the pod borer, which is most severe in Sumatra and Kalimantan.

"We are conducting experiments in Sulawesi on how to contain the pod borer, and the ultimate objective would be to implement the measures throughout the country," he told Reuters by phone from the key growing region of South Sulawesi.
Mumford, deputy director at the centre for environmental technology at the Imperial College, said the experiment, which had completed its first month, was at a preliminary stage.
"The yield loss in the demonstration areas was five percent, compared with 30 to 35 percent outside the demonstration area," he told Reuters by phone from Ujung Pandang, South Sulawesi.
"(But) to get the complete picture, we must take samples for six months," he said.
Mumford said the technique used on the experimental plots involved regular pruning of the cocoa trees, and the regular, frequent and complete harvesting of cocoa pods.

"The farmer must pick all the ripe pods. He has to do it frequently so that he picks them when they are quite young and ripe. You don't keep them on the trees for one month and have caterpillars come out," he said.
"The larva is inside the pod before it is ripe. If you take the pod off the tree and break it to remove the beans, you can kill the larva while you are harvesting," he said.
"But if you leave it on the tree for two or three weeks, the larva comes out and will infest (other pods)."
Mumford said pruning produced an open canopy that could be penetrated by sunshine -- an environment not conducive for moths -- and relatively low trees that made harvesting easy.

"The question (now) is whether we can demonstrate to the farmer in a way that will encourage him to take up these practices," he said. "The practices are very low technology and can be taken immediately."
Mumford said farmers were not already carrying out these measures because of a lack of knowledge.
"They must learn how to do it," he said. "Askindo has agreed to spread the common message...the message is relatively simple," he added.
